title: FANUC Co-Training Module
contentStatus: Built per Content Principles (60% pass, terminology + notes). This module name and rationale are confirmed per CDD - reflects DiFacto's unique position integrating both MoRo and FANUC systems. Specific FANUC curriculum content pending joint development with FANUC-side training materials.

sections.title: Why FANUC Co-Training Exists
learningObjectives: Understand DiFacto's position as an integrator of both MoRo and FANUC systems
Recognize why this makes a dual-system Master Instructor more valuable
sections.content: Many DiFacto deployments involve MoRo working alongside FANUC robotic systems. The I/O handshake integration covered earlier in the Technician and Programmer tracks reflects this reality. A Master Instructor who can train on both MoRo and the FANUC integration points it connects to is a significantly more valuable training resource than one who only knows MoRo in isolation - since real deployments rarely involve MoRo alone.

keyTerms.note: An industrial robotics manufacturer whose controllers MoRo commonly integrates with via I/O handshake.

sections.title: What This Module Covers
learningObjectives: Understand the general scope of FANUC-side knowledge relevant to MoRo instructors
Recognize this is integration-focused training, not full FANUC certification
sections.content: This module isn't a substitute for standalone FANUC certification. It covers the FANUC-side knowledge specifically relevant to training others on MoRo-FANUC integration points: the I/O handshake sequence from the FANUC controller's perspective, common FANUC-side configuration that affects integration behavior, and how to explain the combined system to a learner who may be new to one side or the other. Detailed curriculum content is being co-developed with FANUC-side training materials.

sections.title: Teaching an Integrated System
learningObjectives: Understand the pedagogical challenge of teaching a system with two distinct origins
Recognize strategies for building a coherent mental model across both sides
sections.content: Teaching an integrated MoRo-FANUC workflow is harder than teaching either system alone. A learner needs a coherent mental model spanning both, not two separate, disconnected sets of knowledge. Effective instruction here means consistently connecting the two sides explicitly - what MoRo does, what the FANUC controller does in response, and why - rather than teaching them as parallel but unrelated topics.

sections.title: Common Points of Learner Confusion
learningObjectives: Recognize typical areas where learners struggle with integrated systems
Apply instructional strategies to address these proactively
sections.content: Learners new to integrated systems often struggle most with handshake timing. They need to understand that MoRo and FANUC are each waiting on signals from the other, not acting independently. Anticipating this confusion and addressing it early, with the handshake concept already introduced in L3B-M4 and L4A-M4, gives Master Instructors a known point to reinforce rather than leaving it as an implicit assumption.

sections.title: Co-Delivery Considerations
learningObjectives: Understand what co-delivery with a FANUC-side trainer might involve
Recognize when co-delivery is valuable versus when a single instructor suffices
sections.content: For more complex integration training, co-delivery alongside a FANUC-side trainer may be more effective than one instructor covering both sides alone - particularly for advanced troubleshooting scenarios. This module covers how to plan and coordinate that kind of session. The specific protocol for co-delivery logistics is being finalized as DiFacto's instructor network develops.

sections.title: Certification Implications
learningObjectives: Understand how this module factors into overall Master Instructor certification
Recognize the value this adds to DiFacto's instructor network
sections.content: Completing this module as part of the broader L5 Master Instructor track signals an instructor capable of training on DiFacto's most common real-world deployment pattern - MoRo integrated with FANUC systems, rather than MoRo in isolation. This directly supports DiFacto's positioning as an integrator of both systems, a differentiator competitors without FANUC integration depth cannot easily replicate.

questions.question: Why does FANUC co-training matter for DiFacto's Master Instructors?
options: It doesn't - FANUC and MoRo are unrelated
FANUC training is required by law
Many deployments involve MoRo integrated with FANUC systems, making dual-system instructors more valuable
questions.feedback: Correct. Real deployments often combine both systems, making dual-system instructor capability valuable.

questions.question: Is this module a substitute for standalone FANUC certification?
options: FANUC certification is not relevant here
Yes, it fully replaces FANUC certification
No - it covers FANUC-side knowledge specifically relevant to MoRo integration training
questions.feedback: Correct. This module is integration-focused, not a substitute for full FANUC certification.

questions.question: What makes teaching an integrated system pedagogically harder than teaching one system alone?
options: Learners need a coherent mental model spanning both systems, not two disconnected sets of knowledge
Integrated systems have no additional teaching complexity
questions.feedback: Correct. Building a coherent cross-system mental model is the core instructional challenge.

questions.question: What is a common point of learner confusion with integrated systems?
options: Handshake timing - understanding that both systems wait on signals from each other
questions.feedback: Correct. Handshake timing between the two systems is a frequent source of learner confusion.

questions.question: What does completing this module signal about a Master Instructor?
options: Capability to train on DiFacto's common real-world deployment pattern of MoRo integrated with FANUC
That they no longer need any MoRo-specific knowledge
questions.feedback: Correct. It signals readiness to train on the combined system, not MoRo in isolation.
